newsitem.title: JORDAN: Jordan's Islamists consider election boycott.
newsitem.headline: Jordan's Islamists consider election boycott.

text.p: Jordan's powerful Moslem Brotherhood is threatening to pull out of November parliamentary elections which it fears will be rigged in the government's favour.
The Brotherhood, currently controlling the largest single bloc of seats in Jordan's 80-member parliament, is canvassing grassroots members and may announce its decision within days.
"The Moslem Brotherhood will issue its decision on boycotting or participating in the elections by the end of this week," Islamist deputy Abdul-Moneim Abu Zunt said on Monday.
The issue has exposed a deep rift in Brotherhood ranks.

Islamist doves who say parliamentary representation is the only way to stand up to the government face a tough battle with the swelling numbers of hawks who say the government will always be able to railroad its agenda over parliamentary opposition.
Abu Zunt, a leading member of the pro-boycott camp, said the Brotherhood feared widescale fraud after the government withdrew plans for special electoral identity cards.

He said Islamists should pull out because they could never muster a working majority to effectively oppose government policies, particularly Jordan's 1994 peace treaty with Israel which the Islamists want cancelled.

The Brotherhood's political party, the Islamic Action Front (IAF), holds 15 seats in Jordan's 80-seat lower assembly, making it the largest party in parliament dominated by tribal representatives or small pro-government parties.
But it was easily defeated by the government in a parliamentary vote on ratification of the treaty.
"I support the boycott," Abu Zunt told Reuters. "Even if there are (Islamist) parliamentary members they are weak because at least 60 deputies of the 80 represent the government."
Prime Minister Abdul-Salam al-Majali has not yet picked a date for the polls, due to be held by November, but said they will be fair and on schedule.
The boycott proposal has prompted a sharp response from Islamist doves who say that the IAF would be banished to political obscurity and the whole Islamist movement would lose influence.
IAF secretary-general Ishaq Farhan is reported to have said there is no role for his party outside parliament and he would resign if the decision to boycott the elections was approved.
Bassam al-Amoush, an IAF parliamentary deputy, said Islamists had no alternative but to fight the elections.
"We expect fraud (in the elections). But the movement cannot take decisions on unknown expectations," Amoush said.
"To boycott would be a strategic mistake. The Islamic movement would be dealing itself a blow," he said.

While their counterparts have been marginalised from mainstream politics in other Arab countries, Islamists have played a major role in Jordanian politics, often counterbalancing the influence of secular leftist opposition.
"What will happen to the Islamic movement if it is not in parliament? Will it go back to the mosques?... Will it make a revolution?" Amoush asked.
Amoush said just three months ago a large majority of Brotherhood members approved participation in the elections.

He attributed growing calls for a boycott to "provisional" laws issued by the government during parliament's recess which he said were aimed at undermining the opposition, especially the tough amendments to Jordan's press law passed in May.

"Some in the Brotherhood are upset by the government's measures, including the press law," Amoush said. "But the only place to oppose the (press) law would be in the parliament, so boycotting would not be the way to get the law changed."
